column2: Thus delusion is sevenfold, and again these cling to one another; it becomes of many aspects; now hear its characteristics.
First is the consciousness that is nameless, the stainless of the Self; the vessel of the future names and meanings such as mind and individual.
The waking that stays in seed-form is called seed-waking. This is the ninefold state of awareness; hear now the state of non-waking.
For one newly born, the conviction "I am this, this is mine," abiding in itself, from the prior contemplation, is that waking.
The conviction arisen from another birth, "this I am, this is that of mine," robust, is clearly called great waking.
Whether unfixed or fixed, wholly made of it, the waking mind-kingdom of daydreams is called waking-dream.
By the distinction of the double moon, silver in shell, mirage and the like, waking dream, through practice, becomes many-sorted.
I saw this for a short time, where it does not arise — the reflection of one awakened — is the dream.
Because of the absence of long observation, a great utterance not bloomed; but a long-continued dream appears like waking.
Dream-waking is said to be what flashes even in waking. The abandonment of six states, the dull state of the individual.
Rich in the perception of future suffering, that is called deep sleep; in that state the world dissolves into inner darkness.
These seven states of knowledge have been told by me, O twice-born; each is here hundredfold, with various expressions.
Hear this sevenfold ground of knowledge, sinless one; having known this, one does not again sink into the mire of delusion.
Debaters speak of the grounds of yoga in many ways; to me, these alone are approved and give good.
They know awareness as knowledge, that which has seven grounds; liberation is called the known, beyond the seven grounds.
The ground of knowledge called Good Desire is declared first; the second is Inquiry; the third, Thinning of Mind.
The fourth is Attainment of Sattva, then the one named Non-attachment; the sixth is Contemplation of Things; the seventh is called Turya-gaa.
Within these abides liberation, in which one no longer grieves. Now hear the explanation of these grounds.
Why do I remain a fool? I shall look to scriptures and the good — desire preceded by dispassion is called Good Desire by the wise.
The practice of right conduct preceded by contact with scripture and the good and by practice of dispassion is called Inquiry.
Where by inquiry and good desire attachment to sense-objects grows thin, that is called Thinning of Mind.
By practice of the three grounds, through the sway of detachment, when the mind stands in pure sattva, Attainment of Sattva is declared.
By practice of the four stages, the art of non-contact, with the wonder of firm sattva, is called Non-attachment.
By practice of the five grounds, with firm delight in one's own Self, through non-contemplation of inner and outer things;
awakening by long effort directed by another — the sixth ground is called Contemplation of Things.
By long practice of the six grounds, by non-perception of difference, that steadfastness in one's own nature alone is to be known as the Turya-gati.
This is known among the liberated-while-living as the fourth state; the state beyond Turiya concerns bodiless liberation.
Nidagha, those fortunate ones who have taken refuge in the seventh ground, delighting in the Self, great-souled, have reached the great state.
The liberated-while-living do not sink in the taste of pleasure and pain; they do or do not do something according to the occasion.
Awakened by those at their side, they just follow the conduct handed down from earlier practice, like one risen from sleep.
These seven grounds are the domain of the wise alone; even animals and barbarians, having reached this state of knowledge,
whether embodied or bodiless, are liberated — there is no doubt. Knowledge is the cutting of the knot, and when it exists, there is freedom.
It is of the nature of mere cessation of mirage-water notions and the like. Those who have crossed the ocean of delusion have attained the supreme state.
They abide in these grounds, devoted to attaining their own Self. The means of quieting the mind is called yoga.
It is to be known as sevenfold, and those grounds have been told. The goal of these grounds is the state called Brahman.
Where there is no "you-ness" or "I-ness," no otherness at all; no imagining of things anywhere, no domain of being and non-being.
All quiet, without support, abiding in space, eternal, auspicious, free of disease, without appearance, nameless, causeless.
Neither existent nor non-existent, without middle or end, neither all nor not all; ungraspable by mind and speech; fuller than full, happier than happy.
Without cognition, wholly quiet, extended as self-awareness; the being of all things is nothing other than awareness.
In the relation of seer and seen, the vision in the middle is the form; this state is free of seer, seeing and seen.
When the mind goes from place to place, the interval of the mind in the middle — contemplate the undull awareness, and be of that nature always.
For one not in waking, dream or sleep, whatever is your eternal form, insentient yet not dull — be of that nature always.
Setting aside only the dullness, that which is the heart of a rock, the nature of no-mind — be of that nature always. Abandoning the mind far away, whatever you are, you are; be steady.

First the mind arose from the principle of the Supreme Self; by it this world, a net of conceptions, is spread. Even the void, with the void, O Brahmin, as with the sky, the blueness shines, a lovelier name.

When the mind has melted by the destruction of intention, the mist of the world's delusion dissolves. Clear it shines, as the sky when autumn has come, mere consciousness, one, unborn, primal, infinite within.
A picture without maker or canvas has arisen in the sky; the self-experience without seer, the sight without sleep or dream.
In the witness, even, clear, free of conceptions, the Self of consciousness, worlds are reflected without desire, as in a mirror.
Contemplate with effort, for the quieting of the mind's restlessness: Brahman is one, the space of consciousness, the Self of all, unbroken.
As a single thick rock is covered with lines and sublines, so see here one Brahman covered by the three worlds.
For lack of a second cause, this world is unborn; what was to be known is now known, the wonder to be seen has been seen.
I am at rest, long tired; nothing exists apart from pure consciousness. See me with doubts at rest, with all curiosity gone.
The state of no-mind, the supreme state, with the net of imagination cast away; those alone have reached greatness, with all sins quieted.
The great-minded, of quiet mind, who have attained mindlessness; of the creature who has inquired, whose mind's modifications have melted away;
who ever gives up thinking, whose mind has somehow matured, who abandons the seen, who has reached what is to be given up and what to be accepted;
who ever sees the seer, who does not see the non-seer, who is wakeful in the supreme principle to be known, while alive;
for the sleeper on the path of the world, made of delusion by wealth, through utterly ripe dispassion, even in tasteless and tasty things;
now that the net of worldly impressions, like a bird-net, is broken, the knot of the heart loosened by the force of dispassion;
as water becomes clear on getting the Katakā fruit, so by virtue of knowledge one's nature becomes serene.
Without attachment, without contact, without duality, without support, the mind goes forth from delusion like a bird from a cage.
With doubts and evil nature quieted, with curiosity and confusion gone, the mind, filled within, shines like the full moon.
I am not, nor is there anything else here; I am only Brahman, free of disease — thus whoever sees from the middle of being and non-being, he sees.
As the mind falls without effort on what the eye sees, without attachment, so the steady-minded act in their works.
Enjoyment, after being understood, brings contentment; a thief, known and served, becomes a friend, not a thief.
As a village-journey met without expectation is looked at by travelers, so the wise regard the splendor of pleasures.
Of the restrained mind, even a slight playful enjoyment, as it has no extension, he esteems greatly because of its pain.
A king freed from bondage is satisfied with a mouthful; not bound by others, not attacked, he does not value a kingdom much.
Pressing hand with hand, crushing teeth with teeth, overcoming limbs with limbs, one should first conquer one's own mind.
There is no other way across the ocean of existence than the conquest of the mind; in the empire of great hell, elephants of wrong-doing are in rut.
Rich in arrows and spikes of hope, the enemies of the senses are hard to conquer; for one whose mind's pride has been wasted, who has restrained the foes of the senses,
impressions of enjoyment fade like lotuses in winter. As long as the mind is not conquered by firm practice of the one truth, impressions dwell in the heart like ghouls in the night.
I regard the mind of the discerning as a servant for doing what is wished, a minister for accomplishing all aims, a vassal for the senses' conquests.
I regard the mind of the wise as a loving woman for caressing, a father for protecting, a friend for best counsel.
By one's own light, by the vision of scripture, by one's own intellect, by one's own experience, the mind-father gives the supreme accomplishment, abandoning himself.
Very glad, very firm, clear, well-advanced, well awakened, the jewel of the mind shines pleasing in the heart, strong by its own quality.
O Brahmin, this jewel of the mind, stained by much mud — wash it with the water of discrimination for success, and be one who sees light.
Relying on the highest discrimination and seeing truth by intellect, cut down the enemies of the senses, and cross the ocean of becoming.
They know mere reliance as the mine of endless sorrows; they know mere non-reliance as the abode of all happiness.
This world turns round bound by the thread of impressions; that, famed for great sorrow, becomes happiness when it is cut off.
Even the steady, even the very learned, even the high-born, even the great, a creature is bound by craving, as a lion by a chain.
Taking up supreme human effort and ready exertion, acting according to scripture without agitation, who would not reach success?
I am all this universe, I am the Supreme Self, the undying; there is nothing else — that awareness is the supreme I-sense.
I am distinct from all; I am subtler than a hair's tip — that second I-sense of awareness, O Brahmin, is auspicious.
This is for liberation, not for bondage, for the liberated-while-living.
I am only hands, feet and the like — this conviction is egoism, the third, worldly and petty.
This is the individual, the evil-natured, the bulb of the hard-to-cross tree of the world; struck by it a creature runs ever lower.
By this evil egoism long abandoned in its being, the creature with the remaining egoism and peace goes to liberation.
Accepting the first two egoisms as unworldly, the third egoism, worldly and giving pain, is to be abandoned.
Then, abandoning those too, free of all ego-sense, he stays thus most high and ascends to the supreme.
Bondage is mere desire for enjoyment; its renunciation is called liberation. The rise of the mind is destruction; the destruction of the mind is a great rise.

The mind of the knower goes to destruction; the mind of the ignorant is a chain. Neither bliss nor non-bliss, neither moving nor unmoving, steady, neither existent nor non-existent, nor the middle of these — thus they know the mind of the wise.
As the sky, being subtle, is not noticed as a reflection of consciousness, so the partless state of consciousness, though all-pervading, is not noticed.
Free of all intention, devoid of all names, this indestructible consciousness is given names such as "Self" and the like.
A hundredth part of space, in the knowers of a partless form, seeing the one Self as the whole nature of the pure world.
It neither sets nor rises, neither stands up nor stays; neither goes nor comes; consciousness is neither here nor not here.
This consciousness has a spotless form, free of conceptions, without support.
At first one should purify the disciple by qualities such as calm and self-control; afterward one should teach: "All this is Brahman, you are pure."
Whoever says "all is Brahman" to the ignorant or half-awakened is thereby bound to nets of great hell.
To one of awakened intellect, whose desire for pleasure is exhausted, without hope, the wise teacher should teach: "There is no stain of ignorance."
As light exists when there is a lamp, day when there is a sun, fragrance when there is a flower, so the world exists as truth in consciousness.
This appears only; the world is not ultimately real. When the eye of knowledge is clear and the arising of awakening spreads,
